solution.concept_anchor: Fundamental Duties — 42nd Amendment added 10 duties; 86th added 11th
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who know that Fundamental Duties are generally non-justiciable may assume this is what makes Article 51A(k) different — but non-justiciability applies to all Fundamental Duties, not just 51A(k).
elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute: three of the four items share an attribute related to Article 51A(k) and the 86th Amendment.
Article 51A(k) is correlative to a Fundamental Right (Article 21A) — this is unique; other Fundamental Duties are not correlated to justiciable Fundamental Rights: shared attribute.
Article 51A(k) was added by the 86th Amendment, 2002 — it is the 11th Fundamental Duty: shared attribute.
Article 51A(k) imposes duty on parents/guardians regarding education — shared attribute with the preceding items.

The duty under Article 51A(k) is non-justiciable — but this is NOT unique to 51A(k); ALL Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable. However, option (b) states it applies only to 51A(k) — this scope-extension makes it the odd statement. Among the four items, option (c) — 'inserted by the 42nd Amendment' — is factually wrong for 51A(k) (which was inserted by the 86th Amendment) and is thus the item that does NOT belong.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap substitutes the 42nd Amendment (which added the original 10 Fundamental Duties in 1976) for the 86th Amendment (which added the 11th duty — 51A(k) — in 2002). Students who know that Fundamental Duties were added by a constitutional amendment, without remembering which specific amendment added which duty, will conflate the two amendments. The 42nd Amendment is strongly associated with Fundamental Duties generally, making this substitution feel plausible.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests precision about Article 51A(k) — which amendment added it, and what makes it unique.

• Option (a) — Shares the attribute: Article 51A(k) is directly correlative to Article 21A — the only Fundamental Duty linked to a justiciable Fundamental Right. This is a genuine, unique characteristic.
• Option (b) — Shares the attribute: All Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable under Article 37 (read with their nature as duties, not rights). This correctly describes 51A(k) but is not unique to it — all duties share this character.
• Option (c) — Does NOT share the attribute: Article 51A(k) was inserted by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 — NOT the 42nd Amendment. The 42nd Amendment (1976) added the original ten Fundamental Duties (51A(a) through 51A(j)). This is the odd one out.
• Option (d) — Shares the attribute: The duty under 51A(k) falls on the parent or guardian, not on the child — this is a correct characterisation.

Value Addition:
• The 42nd Amendment added Articles 51A(a) to 51A(j) — ten duties covering national ideals, sovereignty, cultural heritage, and environment.
• The 86th Amendment added only one new duty — Article 51A(k) — the parental duty regarding education.
• Justice Verma Committee (1999) reviewed Fundamental Duties and recommended making some operational through legislation, though comprehensive implementation legislation does not exist.

solution.concept_anchor: RTE Section 13 screening prohibition and school de-recognition consequence

statement_analysis.statement: Section 13 of the RTE Act prohibits schools from subjecting a child or the child's parents to any screening procedure for admission to an entry-level class.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 13 explicitly prohibits both screening procedures and capitation fees at the time of admission to the entry-level class. The prohibition covers the child and the parents — preventing entrance tests, interviews, or prior knowledge assessments.

statement_analysis.statement: The prohibition on screening procedures under the RTE Act applies equally to all classes from entry-level through Class VIII.
statement_analysis.reason: The prohibition on screening under Section 13 applies specifically to admission to the entry-level class. It does not govern admission processes for subsequent classes through Class VIII — the section's scope is admission to the starting grade.

statement_analysis.statement: A school that fails to meet the infrastructure norms prescribed in the Schedule to the RTE Act may face de-recognition.
statement_analysis.reason: Schools that fail to comply with the Schedule's physical norms within the prescribed period (three years from RTE's commencement) face de-recognition — a significant enforcement consequence under the Act.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'all three' is a strong distractor because Statements 1 and 3 are clearly correct, and Statement 2's extension sounds reasonable to a student who assumes that the prohibition on screening, once established for entry, must logically apply to all grades.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — Section 13 prohibits screening at the entry-level class admission stage for both child and parents.
Statement 2 is incorrect — the prohibition applies only to the entry-level class, not all classes up to Class VIII; eliminate options including Statement 2.
Statement 3 is correct — de-recognition is the stated consequence for non-compliance with Schedule norms.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the natural assumption that if screening is banned at entry, it must be banned throughout elementary education. However, the RTE Act's Section 13 is specifically limited to admission to the entry-level class — it addresses the point of initial entry, not lateral transfers or promotion procedures. The scope-extension from 'entry-level' to 'all classes' is the exact trap mechanism.
solution.final_explanation:
Two distinct obligations — the anti-screening provision and the infrastructure compliance mechanism — test precision about the RTE Act's scope.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Section 13 makes it unlawful for any school to subject a child or parent to any screening procedure when seeking admission to the entry-level class. This covers all forms of selection — written tests, oral interviews, or indirect checks like parental qualification assessments.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Section 13 prohibition is explicitly for the entry-level class. For admission to other classes, the Act does not impose the same specific restriction — lateral entry may involve different processes. The scope cannot be extended beyond what Section 13 texts.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The RTE Act's Schedule prescribes minimum physical infrastructure standards. Schools that fail to achieve these within the three-year window (2010–2013) face de-recognition — removal of their legal status to operate as recognised schools.

Value Addition:
• Where seats are limited in the EWS category, a lottery system must be used — no performance-based selection is permitted.
• The capitation fee ban under Section 13 is accompanied by a 10x penalty — the highest deterrent multiple in the Act.
• De-recognition is distinct from closure — a de-recognised school may no longer issue certificates but may continue to exist and seek re-recognition after complying with norms.

solution.concept_anchor: Mohini Jain — right to education at all levels from Article 21
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because Unnikrishnan is also associated with deriving the right to education from Article 21, and students conflate the two cases' holdings on the scope of that right.
elimination_logic: The question asks which case first held that the right to education is a Fundamental Right extending to all levels of education.
Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka (1992) made the broader claim — education as Fundamental Right at all levels.
Unnikrishnan (1993) refined this — restricting the free education right to up to age 14 only; eliminate (a).

Eliminate (c) and (d): The 86th Amendment is a constitutional provision, not a case; T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002) dealt with private educational institutions' rights, not the scope of the right to free education — option (b) is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Unnikrishnan case is more frequently cited in textbooks as the foundational case for education as a Fundamental Right (because it is the more nuanced holding). Students who have read Unnikrishnan more carefully than Mohini Jain will associate the 'right to education from Article 21' holding with Unnikrishnan rather than Mohini Jain. In fact, Mohini Jain (1992) established the broader principle first; Unnikrishnan (1993) came second and restricted it.
solution.final_explanation:
The judicial recognition of education as a Fundamental Right followed a two-step evolution in the early 1990s.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Unnikrishnan J.P. v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993) restricted, rather than broadly established, the right to education. It held that the right to free education was enforceable only up to age 14, linking it to the state's obligation under Article 45 DPSP.
• Option (b) — Correct: Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka (1992) was the first Supreme Court case to hold that the right to education is a Fundamental Right derivable from Article 21 — and at that stage, the Court held it extended to all levels of education, including higher education.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act (2002) is the legislative instrument that constitutionally codified the right — it is not a judicial case.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002) dealt with the right of private educational institutions to establish and administer institutions — a different dimension of the education rights framework.

Value Addition:
• Mohini Jain arose from the capitation fee controversy in private medical colleges — the court connected education access to the right to life and dignity.
• The Unnikrishnan case directly relied on Mohini Jain but used the Article 45 DPSP to limit the free education right to age 14.
• T.M.A. Pai Foundation (11-judge bench, 2002) is significant for defining minority and non-minority private institution rights — foundational for understanding Section 12(1)(c) exemptions.

solution.concept_anchor: RTE teacher deployment restrictions and infrastructure norms

statement_analysis.statement: The RTE Act prohibits the deployment of teachers for any non-educational purpose whatsoever, including election duty and disaster relief operations.
statement_analysis.reason: The RTE Act prohibits deployment of teachers for non-educational purposes except for three specific activities: the decennial census, elections (election duty), and disaster relief. These are carved-out exceptions, not blanket prohibitions.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the RTE Act, a school serving Classes I to V is required to maintain a Pupil-Teacher Ratio of no more than 30 students per teacher.
statement_analysis.reason: The Schedule to the RTE Act prescribes a PTR of 30:1 for Classes I through V — this is a maximum ratio, meaning the school must not have more than 30 students per teacher at the primary stage.

statement_analysis.statement: The RTE Act mandates that schools must provide separate toilet facilities for girls and boys as part of the infrastructure norms in its Schedule.
statement_analysis.reason: Separate toilet facilities for girls is explicitly prescribed in the Schedule to the RTE Act as a non-negotiable infrastructure norm. The absence of girl-specific toilets is a ground for de-recognition.

statement_analysis.statement: Qualifications for teachers under the RTE Act are prescribed by the National Council for Teacher Education (NCTE) acting as the academic authority under Section 23.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 23 of the RTE Act designates the academic authority (the government may notify any body as the academic authority) to prescribe minimum qualifications. NCTE has been so designated for school teachers, giving it the role of specifying teacher eligibility conditions.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is a strong distractor because Statements 2, 3, and 4 are all correct, and Statement 1 is the precision trap — students who know teachers can be called for election duty may not recall that Statement 1 goes further by claiming a blanket prohibition including election duty, making the 'Only three' count attractive.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is incorrect — election duty and disaster relief are explicitly permitted exceptions to the teacher deployment ban; 'whatsoever including election duty' is a false absolute.
Statement 2 is correct — PTR for Classes I–V is 30:1 as prescribed in the Schedule.
Statement 3 is correct — separate girl toilets are mandated in the Schedule.
Statement 4 is correct — NCTE is designated as the academic authority under Section 23 for prescribing teacher qualifications.
Three statements (2, 3, 4) are correct — option (b) 'Only three'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 deploys a scope-extension: the RTE Act does prohibit teacher deployment for most non-educational purposes — but not election duty, census, and disaster relief, which are explicit exceptions. A student who knows 'teachers cannot be used for other purposes' but does not know the specific exceptions will validate Statement 1's blanket claim, miscounting the correct statements.
solution.final_explanation:
The RTE Act's teacher-related and infrastructure provisions involve specific norms and exceptions that are frequently tested at the precision level.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The prohibition on non-educational deployment is not absolute. Three activities are explicitly permitted: the decennial census, election duty, and disaster relief operations. Using teachers for private work, commercial purposes, or routine administrative tasks is prohibited.
• Statement 2 — Correct: PTR of 30:1 for Classes I–V ensures a minimum teaching quality standard. For Classes VI–VIII, the prescribed PTR is 35:1.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Schedule's infrastructure norms include separate and functional toilets for girls — a provision with significant implications for girl child retention in schools.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Section 23 empowers the appropriate government to prescribe qualifications through a notified academic authority. NCTE was designated as this authority, and its Teacher Eligibility Test (TET) is the primary qualification check.

Three statements are correct — option (b).

Value Addition:
• The TET was introduced as a minimum eligibility condition under NCTE norms — states conduct their own TETs (STET) in addition to the Central TET (CTET).
• Untrained teachers were given multiple deadline extensions to acquire qualifications — most recently to March 2019.
• The library is also listed as a mandatory infrastructure norm in the Schedule — schools without a library space face non-compliance notices.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 24 hazardous work only — Child Labour Act 2016 all occupations broader

statement_analysis.statement: Article 24 of the Constitution, as originally enacted, prohibits the employment of children below the age of 14 in factories, mines, and other hazardous employment — but does not extend this prohibition to all forms of child employment.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 24 uses the phrase 'factories, mines, or any other hazardous employment' — the textual scope is limited to hazardous contexts. It does not constitute a blanket constitutional prohibition on all child work below age 14.

statement_analysis.statement: The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2016 restricted the prohibition on child employment to only those sectors classified as hazardous, thereby aligning its scope with Article 24.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2016 Amendment moved in the opposite direction — it expanded the prohibition beyond hazardous employment to cover ALL occupations and processes for children below 14 years. This makes the statutory prohibition broader than Article 24's constitutional text, not narrower or equivalent.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) appears to validate Statement 1 and invalidate Statement 2, which is the correct answer. The distractor effect works on students who misread Statement 2 as saying the 2016 Act expanded coverage (which is true) — the key error is the word 'restricted' which inverts the actual legislative direction.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 24 covers 'factories, mines, and other hazardous employment' — not all employment. This correctly characterises a limitation in the constitutional text. Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: The 2016 Child Labour Amendment Act did not restrict — it expanded — the prohibition to all occupations for under-14. The word 'restricted' in Statement 2 directly inverts the correct position. Statement 2 is incorrect.

Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect → option (c). Wait — option mapping: (a) Both correct, (b) Both incorrect, (c) Statement 1 correct/Statement 2 incorrect, (d) Statement 1 incorrect/Statement 2 correct. Answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses the word 'restricted' — the precise opposite of what the 2016 Amendment did. Students who know that the 2016 Act and Article 24 both use the age-14 threshold may assume the statute 'aligned' with the Constitution by restricting its scope to hazardous work. In reality, Parliament went beyond Article 24's constitutional text — a legislative expansion, not a restriction. Reading the word 'restricted' carefully is the differentiating skill tested here.
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between Article 24's constitutional prohibition and the Child Labour Act's statutory prohibition is one of constitutional floor vs. statutory expansion.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 24's text is limited — it covers factories, mines, and 'other hazardous employment.' The qualifier 'hazardous' restricts its direct scope. Parliament derives authority to go further through legislation under the Concurrent List, but the constitutional text itself does not prohibit all child work.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The 2016 Amendment to the Child Labour Act dramatically expanded the prohibition — making it unlawful to employ any child below 14 in ANY occupation or process, hazardous or otherwise. This is broader than Article 24's constitutional scope. The word 'restricted' in Statement 2 inverts the actual direction of legislative change.

Value Addition:
• The 2016 Amendment also added a new category — 'adolescent' (14–18 years) — prohibiting their employment in hazardous occupations and processes.
• The family enterprise exception allows children to work in non-hazardous family businesses outside school hours — a controversial carve-out in the 2016 law.
• India ratified ILO Convention 138 (minimum age for employment) in 2017, reinforcing the domestic prohibition framework.

solution.concept_anchor: RTE enforcement hierarchy — local authority SCPCR NCPCR roles
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because it correctly places NCPCR at the national level but incorrectly assigns the grievance mechanism's first stage to NCPCR rather than the local authority — a common confusion about where complaints are first filed.
elimination_logic: A (NCPCR) — national-level body designated under Section 31 of the RTE Act for monitoring; its parent statute is the CPCR Act, 2005: matches with 3.
B (SCPCR) — state-level monitoring body under RTE; handles appeals from local authority decisions and monitors state-level implementation: matches with 4.
C (Local Authority) — first stage of the RTE Act's grievance redressal mechanism; complaints about RTE violations are initially made to the local authority: matches with 1.
D (Grievance redressal hierarchy) — complaints go local authority → SCPCR → NCPCR in appellate order: matches with 2. Correct: A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2 — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap places NCPCR as the first-instance grievance authority (option b) rather than the appellate body. Students who know NCPCR is 'the authority for RTE enforcement' may conflate monitoring function with first-instance adjudication. The grievance hierarchy — local authority first, then SCPCR, then NCPCR — requires specific knowledge of Section 32's complaint mechanism distinct from Section 31's monitoring role.
solution.final_explanation:
The RTE Act creates a tiered enforcement and grievance mechanism involving multiple institutions at different levels.

Correct Matching: A–3, B–4, C–1, D–2

• A (NCPCR) — matched with 3: NCPCR is a statutory body established under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005, and designated as the national-level monitoring authority under Section 31 of the RTE Act. It is an appellate body in the grievance hierarchy, not the first port of call.
• B (SCPCR) — matched with 4: State Commissions for Protection of Child Rights function at the state level, monitoring RTE implementation across the state and hearing appeals from local authority decisions.
• C (Local Authority) — matched with 1: Section 32 of the RTE Act requires complaints about RTE violations to be filed with the local authority in the first instance. This is the entry point for grievance redressal.
• D (Grievance redressal appellate sequence) — matched with 2: The hierarchy runs local authority → SCPCR → NCPCR. Each level can hear appeals from the level below.

Value Addition:
• NCPCR was established in March 2007 — two years before the RTE Act came into existence.
• In states that have not constituted SCPCRs, the National Commission may perform state-level functions as well.
• NCPCR has broader child rights jurisdiction: it also monitors POCSO implementation, child trafficking, and juvenile justice — not just education.

Scope and Age Bracket: The '6-14 Years' Limitation

solution.concept_anchor: NEP 2020 policy document — requires RTE Act amendment for legal force
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because NEP 2020 was approved by the Cabinet — a high-level executive act — which students may equate with having legal effect. The scenario's description of a 'child of 4 years' being denied RTE benefits makes the question feel practically urgent, reinforcing the instinct to find a legal remedy.
elimination_logic: The question asks whether a 4-year-old can claim RTE Act benefits based on NEP 2020's proposal to extend coverage to age 3.
Article 21A covers 6–14 years; the RTE Act operationalises this. A 4-year-old falls outside the current statutory and constitutional bracket.
NEP 2020 is a policy document — not legislation. Its proposals do not have binding legal force without a formal amendment to the RTE Act.
Eliminate (a): Cabinet approval makes NEP 2020 government policy, not law — it cannot override the statutory age bracket in the RTE Act.

Eliminate (b) and (d): Early childhood care is under Article 45 DPSP (non-justiciable); there is no Fundamental Right for the under-6 group. Option (c) correctly identifies that NEP 2020 has no operative legal force for this claim without statutory amendment.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is the 'NEP as law' fabrication embedded in option (a). Students who know NEP 2020 was approved by the Cabinet — a significant executive endorsement — may assume it carries the force of a statute. Cabinet approval makes NEP a policy of the government, not an Act of Parliament. Without a formal amendment to the RTE Act, the 6–14 age bracket remains the operative legal boundary, and a 4-year-old has no enforceable Fundamental Right to education under current law.
solution.final_explanation:
The scenario tests the critical distinction between government policy and binding legislation in the context of educational rights.

Scenario Analysis: A parent seeks admission for a 4-year-old child at a government school, arguing that NEP 2020 has extended RTE coverage to age 3.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Cabinet approval gives NEP 2020 the status of government policy — not statutory law. The RTE Act's 6–14 age bracket can only be changed by an Act of Parliament amending the RTE Act itself. A policy document, however authoritative, cannot override a statute.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Pre-school care for under-6 children is governed by Article 45 DPSP — a non-justiciable directive. This does not create a Fundamental Right enforceable in court for a 4-year-old.
• Option (c) — Correct: The parent's claim has no legal basis under current law. The RTE Act's coverage begins at age 6. NEP 2020 is a policy proposal requiring parliamentary action to become law. Until the RTE Act is formally amended, the 4-year-old falls outside the Act's coverage.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Under-6 care is not transferred to Article 21A — it remains in Article 45 DPSP. No constitutional amendment has extended Article 21A's age bracket.

Value Addition:
• The NIPUN Bharat Mission (2021) addresses foundational learning for ages 3–9 but operates as an executive programme, not under the RTE Act.
• Pre-primary education in Anganwadi centres falls under the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) scheme — a separate executive programme under the Ministry of Women and Child Development.
• Amending the RTE Act to incorporate NEP 2020's 3–18 range would also require amending Article 21A — a constitutional amendment — for the under-6 group to acquire Fundamental Right status.

concepts_used: Role of State vs. Central Government: Concurrent List Position

solution.concept_anchor: 42nd Amendment 1976 moved education to Concurrent List — before that State List
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because the 44th Amendment (1978) is in the same approximate era as the 42nd Amendment and is also associated with significant constitutional changes (restoration of property right as legal right), making it a plausible year-era swap.
elimination_logic: The question asks which constitutional amendment moved education from the State List to the Concurrent List.
The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 is the correct answer — it transferred education along with several other subjects.
Eliminate (a): The 44th Amendment (1978) dealt with property rights and emergency provisions — not education's list placement.

Eliminate (c): The 86th Amendment (2002) inserted Article 21A — it did not change education's list placement; eliminate (d): The 52nd Amendment (1985) introduced the anti-defection law — unrelated to education's concurrent status.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 42nd and 44th Amendments are close in time (1976 and 1978) and both are landmark amendments — the 42nd for centralising changes, the 44th for reversing some Emergency-era provisions. Students who associate education's List transfer with 'a major 1970s amendment' without recalling the precise amendment number will be drawn to option (a). The 86th Amendment (option c) is the most tempting for students who associate education exclusively with the 2002 RTE-related amendment.
solution.final_explanation:
The constitutional placement of education in the Concurrent List resulted from one of the most sweeping amendments in Indian constitutional history.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) reversed some Emergency-period changes — notably converting the right to property from a Fundamental Right (Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31) to a legal right (Article 300A). It did not address education's list placement.
• Option (b) — Correct: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 transferred 'education' from Entry 11 of the State List to Entry 25 of the Concurrent List (List III). This was one of several centralising changes made during the Emergency period.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The 86th Amendment (2002) inserted Article 21A and amended Article 45 — changes within constitutional rights structure, not changes to the Seventh Schedule's list placement.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The 52nd Amendment (1985) introduced the Tenth Schedule (anti-defection law) — entirely unrelated to education or the Seventh Schedule lists.

Value Addition:
• Before the 42nd Amendment, Parliament had no direct legislative authority over general education — it could legislate only on specific Union List entries (e.g., education of certain minorities, technical education standards).
• The 42nd Amendment also moved 'forests' and 'weights and measures' to the Concurrent List — all were centralising transfers.
• The Seventh Schedule's List III (Concurrent List) currently has 52 entries — education is Entry 25.

solution.concept_anchor: Society of Unaided Private Schools 2012 — minority exemption scope

statement_analysis.statement: In Society of Unaided Private Schools v. Union of India (2012), the Supreme Court struck down Section 12(1)(c) of the RTE Act as unconstitutional for violating the right to carry on business of private school managements.
statement_analysis.reason: The Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of Section 12(1)(c) in this case — it did not strike it down. The Court held that the state could impose this obligation on unaided non-minority schools without violating any fundamental right of the school management.

statement_analysis.statement: The reimbursement paid by the government to private schools for 25% reserved seats is calculated at the actual per-child expenditure incurred by the private school, regardless of what the government spends in its own schools.
statement_analysis.reason: The reimbursement is the lower of two amounts: either the per-child expenditure incurred by the state in its own schools, or the actual per-child expenditure of the private school. It is capped at the government school's per-child cost — the private school's actual expenditure is not automatically reimbursed.

statement_analysis.statement: Both aided and unaided minority educational institutions are exempt from the 25% EWS reservation under Section 12(1)(c), but are required to comply with all other provisions of the RTE Act.
statement_analysis.reason: The exemption for minority institutions is specifically from the 25% reservation clause — other RTE provisions such as infrastructure norms, teacher qualifications, ban on corporal punishment, and prohibition on capitation fees continue to apply to minority institutions.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'all three' would be chosen by students who do not know the precise outcome of the 2012 case (Statement 1) and who also misremember the reimbursement cap formula (Statement 2).
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is incorrect — the Court upheld, not struck down, Section 12(1)(c) in the 2012 case; this is a factual inversion.
Statement 2 is incorrect — reimbursement is capped at the government school per-child cost; the private school's actual expenditure is not the measure.
Statement 3 is correct — minority schools are exempt only from the 25% clause; other RTE provisions bind them.
Statements 1 and 2 are NOT correct — option (c) '1 and 2' is the answer.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 inverts the outcome of a landmark case — replacing 'upheld' with 'struck down.' Students who know the 2012 case was significant but cannot recall whether it upheld or invalidated the provision will find Statement 1 plausible. Statement 2 adds a reimbursement formula trap — students who know reimbursement exists may not know its cap structure, making 'actual private school cost' sound reasonable.
solution.final_explanation:
The 25% reservation mechanism and its scope has been shaped by two key Supreme Court decisions involving minority and non-minority private schools.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Supreme Court in Society of Unaided Private Schools v. Union of India (2012) upheld Section 12(1)(c) as constitutionally valid. It held that compelling unaided non-minority schools to reserve 25% seats does not violate their fundamental rights. The Court explicitly excluded minority institutions from this obligation.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The reimbursement amount is not based on the private school's actual expenditure. It is the lower of: (i) per-child expenditure in government schools, or (ii) the actual per-child cost in the private school. This cap prevents private schools from recovering high-fee costs through the reimbursement mechanism.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Minority institutions (aided and unaided) are exempt from Section 12(1)(c)'s 25% obligation but remain bound by the RTE Act's other provisions — infrastructure norms, teacher eligibility, anti-corporal punishment rules, and anti-screening provisions.

Statements 1 and 2 are NOT correct — option (c).

Value Addition:
• The 2014 Pramati judgment extended and reaffirmed the minority exemption, specifically covering unaided minority schools under Article 30(1).
• Reimbursement funds for the 25% reserved seats are typically channelled through the state's education budget — delays in reimbursement have been a practical grievance of private schools.
• The capitation fee ban (Section 13) applies to minority institutions as well — this is one provision where the exemption is NOT available.

solution.concept_anchor: SMC 75% parent membership — proportionate representation of disadvantaged sections
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students who know 'SMC includes elected representatives' and 'SMC has parent majority' may confuse 75% with 50%, conflating the RTE norm with general democratic majority conventions.
elimination_logic: The question asks about the proportion of SMC membership that must be parents or guardians under Section 21 of the RTE Act.
Section 21 specifies that at least three-fourths (75%) of the SMC members must be parents or guardians of children enrolled in the school.
Eliminate (a): 'All members' — SMCs also include elected local authority representatives and teachers; 100% parent membership is not prescribed.
Eliminate (c) and (d): 50% and 60% are below the statutory threshold; option (b) — 75% — is the correct proportion.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 75% threshold may be confused with the general 50%+1 majority convention, making option (c) feel like a reasonable democratic standard. Students who conflate 'majority membership' (over 50%) with the RTE Act's specific three-fourths requirement will select option (c). The precise statutory figure — 75%, not a simple majority — is the differentiating knowledge.
solution.final_explanation:
School Management Committees under the RTE Act are designed to ensure community-driven oversight of school functioning, with a specific parent majority requirement.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: SMCs do not consist entirely of parents — they also include elected local authority representatives and school teachers. An all-parent composition would exclude these groups.
• Option (b) — Correct: Section 21 of the RTE Act mandates that not less than three-fourths (75%) of the SMC members must be parents or guardians of children enrolled in the school. This supermajority ensures community voice dominates school governance.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: A 50% parent membership would allow non-parent members to constitute an equal share — this does not meet the Act's 75% floor.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: 60% is between the incorrect options — it is not the statutory threshold specified in Section 21.

Value Addition:
• Within the 75% parent membership, representation must be proportionate to children from disadvantaged and weaker sections — ensuring marginalised communities have a voice.
• SMC members also include elected local authority representatives (panchayat members, urban local body members) — ensuring accountability to elected governance.
• The SMC's key functions include preparing school development plans, monitoring school working, and recommending proper utilisation of grants received by the school.

solution.concept_anchor: Unnikrishnan — right to free education up to 14 linked to Article 45

statement_analysis.statement: Before the 86th Constitutional Amendment, the Supreme Court in Unnikrishnan J.P. v. State of AP held that the right to free education was enforceable only for children up to the age of 14 years, deriving this from the state's obligation under Article 45 DPSP.
statement_analysis.reason: The Unnikrishnan case (1993) used the Article 45 directive — which at that time required the state to provide free education up to age 14 — as the benchmark for defining the judicially enforceable scope of the right to education read into Article 21.

statement_analysis.statement: The 86th Amendment resolved the conflict between Mohini Jain and Unnikrishnan by constitutionally establishing that the right to education extends as a Fundamental Right at all levels of education.
statement_analysis.reason: The 86th Amendment did not validate Mohini Jain's broader holding. Instead, it constitutionally codified the narrower Unnikrishnan position — making education a Fundamental Right only for the 6–14 age group, not at all levels.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 21A, as inserted by the 86th Amendment, makes free and compulsory education a positive obligation on the state — meaning the state must actively provide education, not merely refrain from denying it.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 21A uses the formulation 'The State shall provide' — this is a positive obligation. It differs from Article 21's negative formulation ('no person shall be deprived'), requiring affirmative action from the state.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'all three' is a strong distractor because Statements 1 and 3 are both correct and clearly supportable, and Statement 2 sounds like a reasonable description of what a constitutional amendment should do — 'resolve the conflict' — without specifying that the resolution favoured the narrower Unnikrishnan position.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — Unnikrishnan derived the right's scope from Article 45 DPSP's age-14 mandate and made it enforceable within that boundary.
Statement 2 is incorrect — the 86th Amendment did not extend the right to all levels; it codified the 6–14 bracket, aligning with Unnikrishnan's restricted view, not Mohini Jain's broader one.
Statement 3 is correct — Article 21A's 'state shall provide' formulation is a positive duty — a significant constitutional design choice.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the precision trap: it claims the 86th Amendment resolved the Mohini Jain–Unnikrishnan conflict by endorsing Mohini Jain's broader 'all levels' holding. In fact, the amendment sided with Unnikrishnan's restricted position — limiting the Fundamental Right to 6–14 years. The word 'resolve' in Statement 2 is accurate (the amendment did resolve the conflict) but the outcome described (all levels) is wrong. Students who know the amendment 'settled the debate' may not check which side of the debate it settled.
solution.final_explanation:
The interplay between judicial precedents and the 86th Amendment's constitutional text reveals a careful legislative choice between two competing judicial positions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Unnikrishnan (1993) crafted an interpretive bridge — using Article 45's directive (which then covered children up to 14) to define the judicially enforceable scope of the right to education derived from Article 21. Above age 14, no free education right was recognised as enforceable.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The 86th Amendment resolved the Mohini Jain–Unnikrishnan conflict by constitutionally endorsing the narrower position. Article 21A covers only 6–14 — not all levels of education. Mohini Jain's 'all levels' holding was effectively superseded, not validated.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 21A imposes a positive obligation — the state must provide education, not merely refrain from obstructing it. This distinction matters enormously: positive obligations require resource allocation and active state intervention, unlike negative freedoms that demand restraint.

Value Addition:
• The positive obligation character of Article 21A means courts can mandamus the state to establish schools, hire teachers, and fund education — not merely restrain it from blocking access.
• Higher education remains outside the Fundamental Rights framework — it has no equivalent to Article 21A, leaving access to higher education subject to legislative and executive policy.
• The Unnikrishnan case also introduced the concept of 'educational trust' — private institutions must treat education as a service, not purely a commercial activity.
